sceneFacts.shortVersion: Hoku's "Perfect Day" was originally for her second album.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Hoku's song "Perfect Day" debuted in the opening sequence of Legally Blonde. The track was written by Antonina Armato and was initially intended as the lead single for Hoku's second album. Those involved in the film referred to it as "this little movie," and no one anticipated the song's long-lasting success upon its release.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Costume designer Sophie de Rakoff used her own style for Elle's outfits.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Costume designer Sophie de Rakoff drew on her background as a music video stylist, which influenced her approach to color and fashion for the film. She approached the designs by interpreting characters through her own taste, without overthinking, which she felt contributed to the film's unique look. De Rakoff aimed to visually represent Elle's journey, starting her as a "seemingly vapid, very feminine character" in Los Angeles. Her aesthetic was also "incredibly influenced by vintage fashion," projecting her style onto the characters.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Matthew Davis based Warner on George W. Bush.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Matthew Davis, who played Warner Huntington III, based his character on a former U.S. president. He specifically turned to George W. Bush for inspiration, reading a biography on America’s 43rd president before taking on the role. Warner's background as someone from a well-to-do family with political aspirations aligned with this inspiration.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Harvard Law scenes were filmed in Los Angeles.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The "Harvard Law School" campus scenes were primarily filmed in Los Angeles, not at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Filmmakers created the Harvard campus using a "frankenstein of locations" across Los Angeles. These included the University of Southern California and UCLA, with the exterior patio of UCLA’s Kerckhoff Hall specifically transforming into the Harvard Law School building where Elle picks up her class schedule.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Legally Blonde was originally set at Stanford Law, not Harvard.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The story of Legally Blonde was inspired by author Amanda Brown's experiences at Stanford Law School, and the film was originally set there. However, Stanford declined permission to film, not wanting its image tarnished by the production. Producers then decided to change the setting to Harvard, believing it would be a more alien environment for Elle Woods.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Elle's dog, Bruiser, was played by a Chihuahua named Moonie.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The Chihuahua who played Elle Woods' loyal companion, Bruiser, was named Moonie. Moonie was owned by trainer Sue Chipperton and shot to stardom as Elle's sidekick in the 2001 film. He later reprised his role as Bruiser in the 2003 sequel, "Legally Blonde 2: Red, White and Blonde."

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Elle's pink pen was inspired by the book's author.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The character of Elle Woods was loosely inspired by author Amanda Brown's real-life experiences at law school. While studying law, Brown wrote her letters home on pink paper with her pink furry pen. These 300 pages of letters eventually became the basis of her "Legally Blonde" book, and her manuscript was reportedly chosen by a publisher because it was also written on pink paper.

sceneFacts.longDescription: Elle Woods drove a black Porsche Boxster in the first Legally Blonde movie. She arrived at Harvard's campus in a black Porche, which featured a personalized "22BLONDE" license plate.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: The "bend and snap" was a spontaneous, last-minute addition.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The iconic "bend and snap" scene was a spontaneous invention that almost didn't make it into the film. Producer Marc Platt requested a B-plot for Paulette, and screenwriters Karen McCullah and Kirsten "Kiwi" Smith initially considered a robbery at the salon. After struggling for weeks with crime-related ideas that felt tonally off, McCullah suggested Elle teach Paulette a move to attract the UPS guy. Smith then spontaneously created the "bend and snap" during a drunken moment at a bar.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Selma Blair's Vivian look hid a skin condition.
sceneFacts.longDescription: To achieve Vivian Kensington's "East Coast, like Jackie O" look, Selma Blair's forehead was threaded for the film. This beauty treatment aggravated Blair's dermatitis, a skin condition she then dealt with for years. Vivian's preppy style, including thick headbands and swooping side bangs, was partly a necessity for Blair to cover up her dermatitis.
